hero.subtitle: A local AI assistant I built to keep my tools and conversations on my own machine.

genesis.title: Genesis
genesis.p1: I use AI assistants often, especially to understand code, or unblock an idea. But I did not like depending on a subscription, a remote service, and a data policy I do not really control.
genesis.p2: Sagittarius started from a simple need: an assistant I could run at home, with the models I choose, without sending my conversations elsewhere. I was not trying to build an AI showcase. I wanted a tool clean enough to actually use.
genesis.p3: The project therefore stayed deliberately personal. Each choice comes from a concrete use case: reduce friction, keep control, and avoid adding complexity just to make the project look bigger.

workspaces.title: The experience I built
workspaces.intro: I organised the application around workspaces because I did not want to mix a code question, an email draft, and a more general conversation in the same thread. Each workspace keeps its own context and history.

code.name: Code
code.desc: The workspace I use to explain a piece of code, investigate an error, or ask a technical question without losing the thread of the current project.

mail.name: Mail
mail.desc: A dedicated space for cleaner wording: rewriting a message, keeping a professional tone, or preparing a reply without mixing it with everything else.

calendar.name: Calendar
calendar.desc: A workspace designed for planning and reminders. The goal is to reason over my local calendar without going through an external service.

notes.name: Notes
notes.desc: A workspace still in development for capturing ideas, preparing lists, and making quick notes easier to find again.

privacy.name: Keep the data at home
privacy.desc: The starting point was non-negotiable: conversations had to stay on my machine. Ollama lets me run the model locally, without an application server in between.

model.name: Choose the model for the task
model.desc: I wanted to test Mistral, LLaMA, Gemma, or other models without rebuilding the application. The model becomes a setting, not a fixed dependency.

streaming.name: See the answer arrive immediately
streaming.desc: Even locally, waiting for a full response quickly feels slow. Streaming makes the tool more pleasant because the answer starts taking shape right away.

markdown.name: Read code and notes properly
markdown.desc: Without Markdown and syntax highlighting, the assistant becomes painful to use for code. I treated rendering as a core part of the experience.

theme.name: Build an interface I want to open
theme.desc: Because this is a personal tool, the interface matters a lot. I wrote it in custom CSS to keep control over the details without adding a full UI library.

architecture.title: How local mode works
architecture.intro: Sagittarius is a Vue 3 frontend that communicates directly with a local Ollama instance. I kept the architecture simple because the project did not need an additional backend.

frontend.title: Frontend
frontend.desc: The application is built with Vue 3, the Composition API, and script setup. State stays local to components when possible: each workspace owns its messages and context without forcing a global state library.

ollama.title: Ollama integration
ollama.desc: Ollama exposes a local HTTP API. Sagittarius sends the conversation history to /api/chat, then reads the streamed response to display text as it is generated.

streaming.title: Streaming implementation
streaming.desc: The response arrives as newline-delimited JSON fragments. Each fragment is parsed, appended to the current message, then reflected in the interface without waiting for the full generation to finish.

architecture.note: I could have added a backend to make the architecture look more conventional, but it would mostly have added latency, deployment work, and maintenance. For this project, the important server is already there: Ollama, running on the machine.

vue.name: Vue 3
vue.desc: Composition API, script setup, reactive state

css.name: Custom CSS
css.desc: Hand-written styles to keep the interface light and controlled

ollama.name: Ollama
ollama.desc: Local model runner, streaming HTTP API

streaming.text: This is the part I underestimated the most. Getting a streamed HTTP response to render live in the DOM was far from intuitive — the reply arrives as a flood of JSON fragments, and my first attempts either re-rendered the whole message on every chunk (visibly janky) or dropped fragments along the way. It took several rewrites before the text appeared smoothly, with the scroll staying at the bottom during generation without trapping me there when I scrolled up to re-read.

state.text: Managing multiple independent conversation threads without a global state library pushed me to think carefully about component ownership. Each workspace owns its history as a local ref, kept alive across router navigation.

product.text: The hard part was not only making local AI work, but reducing the small frictions that make you abandon a tool after two days. A personal project is unforgiving: if something gets in the way, I feel it every time I use it.

css.text: Designing a token system from the start (spacing, type scale, colour variables) made each new workspace significantly faster to build without drifting from the overall feel.

status.title: Where the project stands
status.current: Sagittarius is usable in its current state, especially for code, writing, and general conversations. It is still evolving: some ideas are already integrated, others are still only sketches or prototypes.

next1.title: Calendar workspace
next1.desc: The next planned workspace. Will integrate with local calendar data to allow scheduling, reminders, and natural language event management.

next2.title: File attachment support
next2.desc: Ability to drop a file into the conversation and have the model reason over its content — useful for code review, document summarisation, and data analysis.

next3.title: System prompt per workspace
next3.desc: Each workspace would carry a customisable system prompt, making the assistant's behaviour more targeted without requiring the user to repeat instructions.

status.reflection: This project changed how I think about tools I build for myself. The bar for daily-use software is much higher than for a demo. Every rough edge becomes friction you feel every day.

hero.title: Innov Crous
hero.location: CROUS BFC · Learning Centre Claude Oytana · Besançon / Dijon

context.title: Context & Mission
context.description1: I completed a 15+ week internship within the Animation Numérique et Innovante & Low-Tech (ANI & Low-Tech) service of the Crous Bourgogne Franche-Comté, based at the Learning Centre Claude Oytana in Besançon. The service's mission is to develop innovative activities for students, leveraging a Fablab, a VR immersion room, and a Serious Game Lab.
context.description2: The internship's guiding theme , 'Innov Crous: Making digital attractive at the heart of student residences' , responds to a need to modernise the Crous's image. The goal is to transform often complex administrative processes into fluid, immersive, and collaborative experiences for students.
context.pillar1Desc: Development of Open3D-Viewer, a web-based 3D viewer with VR support for the immersion room.
context.pillar2Desc: Technical support on the IA Annie project, a local administrative AI assistant for Crous users.
context.pillar3Desc: Project lead at the UTBM Crunch Time, a co-design event with students.
context.missionText: All projects follow a deliberate low-tech philosophy: simple solutions, low resource consumption, no dependency on external cloud services, prioritising sustainability and cost control.

org.title: Host Organisation
org.description: The internship took place within a three-level institutional ecosystem, each playing a distinct role across the projects.
org.entity1Desc: Public institution under the Ministry of Higher Education. Manages student housing, catering, and campus life across Besançon, Dijon, Belfort, Montbéliard, and Le Creusot.
org.entity2Desc: Cultural and digital service of the Crous, led by Michel HAVOT. Covers digital support, Fablab management, Serious Game Lab, and organisation of the International Gaming Cities events.
org.entity3Desc: Daily work location, a Crous/University partnership. Houses the VR room, Fablab, Serious Game Lab, and collaborative workspaces open to the university community.

open3d.title: Open3D-Viewer
open3d.description: No tool existed to load and display scientific 3D models directly from a web browser in VR mode within the immersion room. The need was expressed by geology researchers (high-resolution PLY/OBJ formats) and by teaching staff in medicine and sports sciences (interactive 3D anatomical presentations for lectures).
open3d.tech1Desc: Rather than building from scratch, the approach was to fork open3dviewer from the Leiden University Medical Centre, built on BabylonJS. Low-tech approach: no build tool, CDN-only loading. Hosted as moonlight58/open3D-viewer under GPL-3.0 licence.
open3d.tech2Desc: Open-source JavaScript 3D rendering engine. The WebXR standard API enables VR mode directly in the browser without installation. Compatible with the Oculus Quest 2 headsets in the immersion room.
open3d.challenge1Desc: The original project only supported GLB. Adding BabylonJS's additional loaders revealed significant constraints: PLY for Gaussian Splatting requires a very specific schema (Spherical Harmonics, rotation quaternion, encoded opacity). EXR textures are not natively supported for standard meshes.
open3d.challenge2Desc: VR headsets only accept WebXR in a secure HTTPS context, making standard local HTTP testing impossible. Solution: using ngrok to create a public HTTPS tunnel to the local development server.
open3d.deliverable1Desc: Loading GLB, PLY, and OBJ models via URL parameter, tested with real geological models.
open3d.deliverable2Desc: Rotation, zoom, and pan via mouse, keyboard, and touch. Compatible with mobile and tablet.
open3d.deliverable3Desc: Functional WebXR mode, tested in real conditions with the immersion room's Oculus Quest 2 headsets.
open3d.deliverable4Desc: Toggle interface to show/hide sub-parts of a model. Particularly useful for anatomical structures.
open3d.repoDesc: Open source project under GPL-3.0 licence, available on GitHub:

annie.title: IA Annie
annie.description: Annie is a local AI designed to assist students and staff with Crous administrative tasks (housing, grants, service information). Deployed on the Crous infrastructure with no cloud dependency, it addresses data sovereignty and operational cost requirements.
annie.infra1Desc: Local language model inference server, runs without cloud services
annie.infra2Desc: Open-source web interface for interacting with Ollama
annie.infra4Desc: Container orchestration for the production stack
annie.contrib1Desc: Set up and documented a stable shared development environment for the team
annie.contrib2Desc: Documentation of the dev stack (Docker) and production stack (Kubernetes)
annie.contrib3Desc: Performance measurements of Mistral 3B in CPU-only mode (5 runs per protocol)
annie.contrib4Desc: Art direction document and creation of animated SVG assets for the Annie mascot
annie.perfDesc: The analysis measured response times in CPU-only mode, consistent with the Low-Tech prototyping philosophy. Three measurement families, five runs each, medians sourced directly from the Ollama API.
annie.mascotDesignDesc: A red cat (#E30613, the official Crous logo colour) , an animal universally perceived as approachable and calming. A cat actually lived on the Crous campus before being adopted, grounding the character in an authentic local story. A puzzle piece evokes the ANI service's mission around games and cooperation. Three vector SVG assets created: neutral, open mouth, closed mouth , the latter two form an alternating animation simulating speech during generation.

crunch.title: Crunch Time · UTBM
crunch.description: I represented Crous BFC as a project lead at the Montbéliard Crunch Time, an event organised by UTBM. This hackathon-ideation format brings together students from various programmes around projects submitted by partner organisations.
crunch.obj1Desc: Submit the Innov Crous projects to evaluation by the target audience (students) to identify unanticipated features and usability issues.
crunch.obj2Desc: Represent the ANI & Low-Tech service externally, and practice communicating technical projects to a non-specialist audience.
crunch.outcomeText: Feedback gathered during co-design workshops directly fed into the service's roadmap: new features identified, blind spots surfaced, directions refined. The project lead role mobilised communication and facilitation skills distinct from software development.

learning.title: Review & Learnings
learning.technical1: Mastery of BabylonJS for 3D web development (rendering engine, WebXR, loader management)
learning.technical2: Handling complex 3D formats (GLB, PLY, OBJ) and their specific constraints
learning.technical4: Performance analysis of a local LLM: rigorous measurement protocol, interpretation of Ollama metrics
learning.technical5: Using ngrok for VR testing in a secure environment
learning.soft1: Full end-to-end autonomy on a development project
learning.soft2: Effective contribution to a collective project (IA Annie) without being the lead
learning.soft3: Communicating technical projects to a non-specialist audience
learning.soft4: Direct contact with end users and adapting to real usage needs
learning.reflectionDesc: This internship confirmed that technical quality alone is not enough , ergonomics and fit to users' real needs are equally essential. Managing three projects simultaneously at very different levels of responsibility , lead developer, contributor, project lead , was the main challenge and the main richness of this experience.

hero.title: Euphron
hero.location: Learning Centre Claude Oytana • Besançon, France

context.title: Context & Objectives
context.subtitle: Project mission and stakes
context.description1: I had the opportunity to work as a web full-stack intern at the Learning Centre Claude Oytana in Besançon, France, from April 2025 to May 2025. My mission was to create a mobile application called 'Euphron', enabling students at the Université de Franche-Comté to give or take second-hand sports equipment on a donation system.
context.description2: The creation of this application was proposed by STAPS students, following a market study on access to sports equipment in their curriculum. This study revealed that, while some schools manage to provide the necessary equipment to their students, in many others, students themselves must finance their equipment.
context.constraintText: No monetary gain allowed - everything had to be free, based on student solidarity.

role.title: My Role
role.subtitle: Responsibilities & autonomous development
role.description: I was tasked with creating the entire web application (computer and mobile compatible) completely autonomously.
role.responsibility1Desc: Design on Figma for client validation

organization.title: Organization
organization.subtitle: Planning & methodology
organization.methodologyDesc: Weekly meetings with the library team and my internship supervisor. Using Git for versioning and Trello for task management.

techStack.title: Tech Stack
techStack.subtitle: Technologies & architecture
techStack.justificationDesc: I favored Vue.js because I master this framework well, unlike Angular or React. Quasar was the ideal choice for native mobile compatibility, perfectly meeting the project requirements.

features.title: Features
features.subtitle: Development & implementation
features.highlightDesc: Developing the real-time chat with Socket.IO was a first for me. The excellent documentation allowed me to quickly understand the concepts and successfully implement this feature.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.subtitle: Technical structure & data flow
architecture.diagramCaption: Diagram of the communication flow between the frontend (Vue/Quasar) and the backend (Express, Socket.io, MySQL).
architecture.description: The application architecture is based on a clear separation between the frontend, developed with Quasar/Vue.js, and the backend, built around Express, Socket.io and MySQL.
architecture.section1Desc: When a user interacts with the interface via their browser, their actions are handled by Vue components, which orchestrate the display and logic of the application. These components, when they need to access data or trigger server-side operations, call on dedicated JavaScript services.
architecture.section2Desc: In parallel with this traditional operation, the application also integrates a real-time dimension thanks to Socket.io. For features like chat or instant notifications, Vue components communicate with the server via the Socket.io client.

security.title: Security
security.subtitle: Protection & best practices
security.intro: During development, I learned the importance of securing against SQL injections. I implemented double protection:
security.method1Desc: This frontend method checks that the user is not trying to harm the application's operation using a regular expression. This expression verifies that fields (name, email, phone) do not contain suspicious characters like ' " ; -- / * , etc.
security.method2Desc: Prepared (or parameterized) queries offer robust protection because they:
security.method2Item2: Are supported by all modern SQL engines
security.method2Item3: Form the basis of all modern ORMs

learning.title: Learning
learning.subtitle: Skills & feedback
learning.technical2: Deepening web security (SQL injections, prepared queries)
learning.soft1: Autonomy in managing a complete project
learning.reflectionTitle: If I had to do it again
learning.reflectionDesc: I would have preferred working in a team for more efficiency. Being alone, I couldn't implement as many features as desired, although it allowed me to develop my autonomy and ability to manage a project in its entirety.
